prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown. You can look at the current English page with search and read. Use them when what to do in Swedish depends on what that page says outside the diff: above all, whether something a change removed or renamed is still mentioned anywhere on it.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

The rest of that file is not shown.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown. You can look at the current English page with search and read. Use them when what to do in Swedish depends on what that page says outside the diff: above all, whether something a change removed or renamed is still mentioned anywhere on it.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown. You can look at the current English page with search and read. Use them when what to do in Swedish depends on what that page says outside the diff: above all, whether something a change removed or renamed is still mentioned anywhere on it.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

/>

  align="left"
  body={"Acme hjälper dig som arrangerar turneringar att enkelt och smidigt ge en fantastisk helhetsupplevelse till dina deltagare.   divider={true}
  contained={true}
/>

  eyebrow="ENKLA BETALLÖSNINGAR"
  title="Ta enkelt betalt med kort, Klarna eller Swish"
  ctaText="Läs mer om vår betallösning"
  ctaLink="/sv/kort-och-klarna/"
  image="/media/home/klarna_acme-3.webp"
  imageAlt="Betalning med Klarna i Acme"
  imagePosition="right"
  bgColor="light"
  imageFocus="left center"
>
  Med vår moderna betallösning kan ni slippa alla bankbetalningar. Låt lagen betala med kort eller Klarna vilket gör att betalningarna registreras automatiskt i systemet och ni får era pengar direkt.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-2c8d91e4"
  eyebrow="Smartare schemaläggning med AI"
  title="Så fungerar det i Acme"
  ctaText="Läs mer om AI i Acme här"
  ctaLink="/sv/vara-ai-losningar/"
  image="/media/home/ai-image-copy-1.webp"
  imageAlt="AI-schemaläggning i Acme"
  imagePosition="left"
  bgColor="white"

  eyebrow="VI ÄR STOLTA ÖVER VÅR SUPPORT"
  title="Support i världsklass"
  ctaText="Läs mer om vår support här"
  ctaLink="/sv/support/"
  image="/media/home/support.webp"
  imageAlt="Acme-supporten"
  imagePosition="left"
  bgColor="white"
>

</CmFeatureRow>

  imagePosition="right"
  bgColor="light"

  image="/media/home/usp-mobile-app.jpg"
  imageAlt="Egen mobilapp för turneringen"
  imagePosition="left"
  bgColor="white"

</CmFeatureRow>

  imagePosition="right"
  bgColor="light"

</CmFeatureRow>

  align="left"

    heading="Viktiga funktioner"
  >

    </TextBlock>
    <CmButton id="btn-31f7a9d0"
      label="Läs mer om våra funktioner"
      href="/sv/missa-inte/"
      variant="green"
      icon="none"
    />
  </CmColumn>
  <CmColumn id="col-59a3e8d7"
    heading="Prissättning"
  >
    <TextBlock id="text-c21f80b4">
      Vi har en enkel prissättning som passar både små och stora turneringar i olika sporter. Förutom en lagbaserad licens finns det många extratjänster att välja till!
    </TextBlock>
    <CmButton id="btn-e40b97c3"
      label="Läs mer om våra priser"
      href="/sv/priser/"
      variant="green"
      icon="none"
    />
  </CmColumn>
</CmColumns>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-06c9e3b8"
  eyebrow="TA BETALT FÖR FÖRENINGEN"
  title="Acme Clubs"
  ctaText="Läs mer om Acme Clubs"
  ctaLink="https://clubs.acme.example/"
  image="/media/home/si.jpg"
  imageAlt="Acme Clubs"
  imagePosition="right"
  bgColor="light"
>
  Vår systerprodukt Acme Clubs används av uppemot 1000 klubbar för att samla in träningsavgifter och medlemsavgifter, i både Norge och Sverige. Systemet låter dig anpassa er insamling samtidigt som det är väldigt lättanvänt.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-f15b72a0"
  eyebrow="IDROTT ÄR VIKTIGT I EN GLOBAL VÄRLD"
  title="Gemenskap, hopp och utveckling – både här hemma och i Östafrika."
  ctaText="Läs mer om samarbetet"
  ctaLink="/sv/lakeside-youth-cup/"
  image="/media/home/LakesideYouthCup.webp"
  imageAlt="Lakeside Youth Cup"

>
  Vi samarbetar med Lakeside Youth Cup (LYC), en årlig ungdomsfestival i Tanzania som stärker unga genom idrott, utbildning och samhällsengagemang.

Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown. You can look at the current English page with search and read. Use them when what to do in Swedish depends on what that page says outside the diff: above all, whether something a change removed or renamed is still mentioned anywhere on it.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown. You can look at the current English page with search and read. Use them when what to do in Swedish depends on what that page says outside the diff: above all, whether something a change removed or renamed is still mentioned anywhere on it.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown. You can look at the current English page with search and read. Use them when what to do in Swedish depends on what that page says outside the diff: above all, whether something a change removed or renamed is still mentioned anywhere on it.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown. You can look at the current English page with search and read. Use them when what to do in Swedish depends on what that page says outside the diff: above all, whether something a change removed or renamed is still mentioned anywhere on it.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have the content from when Swedish was last synced and a diff showing what changed since then.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

  contained={true}
/>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-2c8d91e4"

  title="How it works in Acme"
  ctaText="Read more about AI in Acme here"
  ctaLink="/en/vara-ai-losningar/"
  image="/media/home/ai-image-copy-1.webp"
  imageAlt="AI scheduling in Acme"
  imagePosition="left"
  bgColor="white"
>
  Building a match schedule that actually works is a complex puzzle – especially with hundreds or thousands of matches, multiple venues, rest periods and special requests to consider.
</CmFeatureRow>

<CmFeatureRow id="feat-7f04b3a9"
  eyebrow="CASE STUDY: FJORDBY BASKET FESTIVAL"
  title="One of our customers shares their story"
  ctaText="Read about Fjordby Basket Festival here"
  ctaLink="/en/fjordby-basket-festival/"
  image="/media/home/customer-story.png"
  imageAlt="Fjordby Basket Festival"
  imagePosition="right"
  bgColor="light"

  image="/media/home/support.webp"
  imageAlt="The Acme support team"

  bgColor="white"

</CmFeatureRow>

  eyebrow="SIMPLE PAYMENT SOLUTIONS"
  title="Accept card, Klarna or Swish payments with ease"
  ctaText="Read more about our payment solution"
  ctaLink="/en/kort-och-klarna/"
  image="/media/home/klarna_acme-3.webp"
  imageAlt="Payment with Klarna in Acme"
  imagePosition="right"
  bgColor="light"
  imageFocus="left center"
>

</CmFeatureRow>

  eyebrow="ENGAGE YOUR VISITORS"
  title="Your own mobile app for Android and iPhone"
  ctaText="Get an app for your tournament"
  ctaLink="/en/app/"
  image="/media/home/usp-mobile-app.jpg"

  bgColor="white"

    heading="Pricing"

    <CmButton id="btn-e40b97c3"
      label="Read more about our pricing"
      href="/en/priser/"
      variant="green"
      icon="none"

  ctaText="Read more about Acme Clubs"
  ctaLink="https://clubs.acme.example/"
  image="/media/home/si.jpg"
  imageAlt="Acme Clubs"
  imagePosition="right"
  bgColor="light"
>

</CmFeatureRow>

  title="Community, hope and growth – both at home and in East Africa."

  bgColor="light"
>

</CmFeatureRow>

Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown. You can look at the current English page with search and read. Use them when what to do in Swedish depends on what that page says outside the diff: above all, whether something a change removed or renamed is still mentioned anywhere on it.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown. You can look at the current English page with search and read. Use them when what to do in Swedish depends on what that page says outside the diff: above all, whether something a change removed or renamed is still mentioned anywhere on it.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.

prompt.system:
You are keeping the Swedish (sv) translation of a document up to date. Its source is English (en): Swedish was translated from it, and has since been corrected and localized by hand. Since Swedish was last brought up to date, someone changed the English page. For each language that changed, you have a diff showing what changed since Swedish was last synced: a line starting with a space is unchanged context, "-" was removed, "+" was added. The rest of that file is not shown. You can look at the current English page with search and read. Use them when what to do in Swedish depends on what that page says outside the diff: above all, whether something a change removed or renamed is still mentioned anywhere on it.

Your job is not to translate the diff. It is to understand each change (what it says, and why it was likely made: a new fact, a correction, a rewording, a removal, a reordering) and then ask: if the person who made it had been editing the Swedish version instead, what would they have changed there? Make those changes.

The versions are not copies of each other. They may differ on purpose: wording, order, examples, local services and links, whole sections that only one language has. Keep all of that, except where a change is about it. It follows that:
- One change may need several edits in Swedish: everywhere Swedish says what changed, also where the other language never said it, so that Swedish does not contradict itself.
- A change may need no edit at all: when Swedish does not have the content it is about, or already says what the change says.
- A change to order or structure applies only where Swedish follows that order or structure.
- Something that only looks like the changed content, but is about something else, stays as it is.

Some things the documents cannot settle: two languages say different things about the same fact, or a change could mean two different things for Swedish. Then do not guess. Call ask, once, with the question, the options you see, and what you would do if no one answered, and keep the content in question as it is unless you get an answer. Ask only when the answer changes what you write, never about wording or style.

Markup is not text. Component and attribute names, ids, front matter keys, file paths and URLs stay exactly as they are, except a link whose Swedish pages follow a convention of their own (a language prefix, a translated path): new links in Swedish follow that convention too. Text a reader sees is Swedish, written as a Swedish writer would put it, not word for word.

Before you edit, write out briefly: for each change, what it says and why it was likely made; then every place in the Swedish file that it concerns, quoted, with whether that place needs an edit and why. Places the other language never mentions count too.

Then make the edits, together in one response. Edit with edit_file: its old_string must appear exactly, once, in the Swedish file. Each edit's result shows the Swedish file around it as it now reads. Look at it: if anything there is wrong, was missed, or now contradicts something elsewhere in the Swedish file, fix it with further edits. When the Swedish file is right, say in a sentence or two what you changed and why. If nothing needs to change, make no edit at all, and say why not. Write your plan, your notes and your summary in English, whatever language the documents are in.
